rows.source: China’s STCW approval date and seafarer training alignment
rows.usage: Paraphrase of extracted passage, CMR51-N095. China became party when STCW entered into force on April 28, 1984 and its training programs are largely aligned with current standards.
rows.finding:
**Open-claim evidence follow-up, November 22, 2026 — Reviewed; unresolved.** The UN registration and IMO status record distinguish China’s June 8, 1981 approval from entry into force on April 28, 1984. Those dates corroborate participation chronology. They do not demonstrate that every current national training programme implements a particular amended STCW standard. Treaty membership, national curriculum requirements and observed compliance are distinct evidence levels.

**Remaining gap or scope limit.** The applicable curriculum/amendment set and implementation evidence for the report’s broad training-alignment claim.

**Earlier audit record (preserved).** Reviewed November 13, 2026. The IMO status book records China’s approval on June 8, 1981 and entry into force on April 28, 1984. It documents later amendments. These entries establish treaty dates. Measuring program alignment requires comparison of curricula, certification and implementation evidence against a specified edition. Follow-up review, November 15, 2026. The IMO convention history distinguishes the original instrument from subsequent amendments. Treaty entry into force is established independently of course-level compliance. A national implementation review still needs a dated training standard and evidence of its application. Source recheck. The UN treaty registration table independently records Chinese approval on June 8, 1981 and effect for China on April 28, 1984. Cite both when distinguishing the instrument date and entry into force. Course-level alignment remains open pending the applicable national curriculum and implementation evidence for the specified STCW amendment set.
evidence: IMO Status of Conventions, STCW 1978 participant table and amendments

**Remaining gap or scope limit.** A transparent minimum-path calculation and a representative career-duration distribution for the typical-experience comparison.

**Earlier audit record (preserved).** Reviewed November 14, 2026. The cited promotion guide and certification regulation describe the sequence of qualifications and sea service. They supply no representative elapsed-time distribution. Separate a modeled minimum from the claim about typical career length. Follow-up review, November 15, 2026. Minimum service periods and the order of qualifying certificates explain how a model could yield an eight-to-ten-year route. They do not measure waiting time, repeated examinations or actual promotions. Representative career data are needed to assess the comparison with typical progression.

rows.source: China accounts for about one third of the world's seafarers.
rows.usage: Paraphrase of original passage. CMR-51, printed p. 2, opening sentence, n. 1. China accounts for about one third of the world's seafarers.
rows.finding:
**Open-claim evidence follow-up, November 22, 2026 — Reviewed; unresolved.** The ICS global estimate is for internationally trading merchant ships. The transport ministry separately counts all registered Chinese seafarers, including inland and coastal categories, and an international-voyage subset. The chapter’s first note cites a trade-site ranking rather than a matched global supply table. A one-third fraction cannot be established by dividing unlike populations or years; the linked trade account itself contains inconsistent percentage language.

**Remaining gap or scope limit.** A same-year China/global table for the same internationally trading workforce, with registered supply distinguished from actually deployed personnel.

**Earlier audit record (preserved).** Reviewed November 14, 2026. The cited industry ranking page could not be opened. BIMCO/ICS estimates 1,892,720 people serving on internationally trading ships worldwide. That denominator uses active service and requires a Chinese numerator for the same year and population. Comparisons with China’s registered pool cannot establish the share. Follow-up review, November 15, 2026. China’s transport ministry publishes registered and deployed workforce measures in its development report. Compare a China numerator for internationally trading ships in the BIMCO/ICS reference year before assigning a global share. A current administrative register is a different population.
evidence: Marine Insight ranking cited in note 1
Ministry of Transport seafarer development report announcement

Shanghai MSA points to a searchable listing by training project. A dated national extract matching the report’s 242 and a consistent definition of an institution were not recovered, so the change remains unverified. Source recheck. The MSA licensing implementation rules distinguish an institution’s current permissions by specific training project and set a December 2025 compliance deadline for organizations already holding authorization. A publicly issued wage reference table distinguishes bulk/general cargo, container, and tanker/chemical categories for the same period. It gives a comparator for cross-sector levels, but those levels cannot establish the growth ranking asserted for a different period. Comparable role- and contract-specific time series are still needed.

paper_memo.memo_title: One-Page Analytical Memo — CMR-51: The Seafarer Profession in Contemporary China (Conor M. Kennedy, Feb 24, 2026)

sections.heading: 1. Strategic Context & Core Thesis
sections.body: Published as China Maritime Report No. 51 by CMSI researcher Conor M. Kennedy, this report treats Chinese merchant mariners as a strategic resource: they crew the world’s largest commercial fleet and would man the civilian lift that the PLA relies on for sealift in a Taiwan contingency. Kennedy’s core finding is a gap between registration and documented service. In 2023, about 47% of the 943,954 mariners registered for international and coastal service had approved sea service. The report also describes a post-2020 turn from oversupply to emerging shortage, and state-specific controls (ship Party branches, political commissars) that are unique to Chinese state-owned shipping.

sections.heading: 2. Section-by-Section Analytical Breakdown
sections.body:
• Fleet (pp. 2–5, Figure 1): 3,051 ships / 225.832 million DWT as of 31 Dec 2024, of which 2,634 are in state-owned companies, led by COSCO Shipping Group (1,535 ships) and China Merchants Group (546).
• Labor supply and demand (pp. 9–14): Figure 3 distinguishes the 2023 international and coastal registration total from the share with approved sea service. The discussion also covers the 2014–2018 sea-time ratio falling from 56.94% to 47.31%, the 2020–2021 shift to shortage, and retention data (about 15,000 maritime-school enrollees a year, a third of whom obtain third-officer or fourth-engineer certificates).
• Pay (pp. 14–15): third officers on major container lines rose from about $1,900 a month in 2019 to $4,700 in 2021; a 7% minimum base-salary increase for 2022–2023; wages receded after zero-COVID ended in January 2023 and owners turned to cheaper foreign ‘mixed manning’.
• Party control and veterans (pp. 9–10, 27–29): Party branch of the ‘Three Chiefs’ led by the political commissar; ‘Project Wave Break’ (2020) veteran placement and its overlap with maritime militia recruitment.

sections.heading: 3. Key Doctrinal Concepts, Terminology & Quantitative Claims
sections.body:
• Registered mariners (注册船员): about 1.98 million at end-2023 across all trades, versus 943,954 for international and coastal routes.
• Approved sea service (海上服务资历): 443,800 of 943,954 international and coastal registrants (about 47%) in 2023. The 2024 Maritime Safety Administration table uses an international-route cohort and gives three distinct counts: 701,308 registered, 418,568 with valid competency certificates and 320,119 with valid certificates and sea service within five years (CMR51-R02, CMR51-R20).
• Ship Party Branch / Three Chiefs (三长): political commissar (secretary), captain (deputy secretary), chief engineer (member).
• Project Wave Break (浪花计划): 2020 Ministry of Transport and Ministry of Veterans Affairs program (1,900 + 1,200 planned veteran placements in 2020).
• Freelance (自由船员) versus in-house (自有船员) seafarers: Note 39 cites a 2024 estimate of about 70%. The estimate’s workforce denominator and treatment of agency contracts need verification. An earlier estimate of roughly 80% is also open (CMR51-R45).

sections.heading: 4. Audit Assessment & Analytical Significance
sections.body:
The initial four claim audits supported the main figures they checked. Row [CMR51-R01] carries three kinds of minor footnote slips (Note 6 browser prefix, Note 9 date, Notes 21 and 23 ‘utm_source=chatgpt.com’). The report’s main figures reconcile arithmetically (Figure 3 totals; 47% sea-service ratio; 2014 and 2018 sea-time percentages).

**Comparing workforce figures**: Identify the trade or route, year, credential status and service window for each count. The 2024 report’s five-year sea-service count and its separate one-year activity measure answer different questions. To test the claim that China accounts for about one third of the world’s seafarers, use a Chinese headcount of people serving on internationally trading ships for the same reference year as the global estimate (CMR51-R20, CMR51-R47).

**Footnote rows**: all 176 footnotes were extracted and consolidated into 140 source rows in the Reference Audit Matrix (CMR51-N001 to CMR51-N176). Repeat citations of the same source within this paper, including Ibid. and short-form notes, share one row, which lists each note's passage and result. Footnote-level result: 176 notes: 44 (25%) are confirmed, 7 of them against a retrieved source and 37 after an outside web search (27 of the latter with a slip or an unchecked detail noted); 2 are flagged for reader check; 132 (75%) are not confirmed. Of the 132 notes not confirmed, 69 are Chinese-language sources that have not been searched in Chinese (a search in Chinese could settle some of them); 6 were judged not web-checkable (4 notes that are fragments or run-on text attached to a Chinese-language source; 2 notes that are explanatory text or a fragment, not a citation); 57 were searched on the web without finding corroboration. A source row is `ok` only when every note in it is confirmed, and `fix` when a note is confirmed wrong; the paper's 140 source rows are 33 `ok`, 0 `fix` and 107 `unk`. Notes flagged for reader check, for example (the outside search found something a reader should look at; none is a finding that the author is wrong): `CMR51-N046`: Figure 3 prints 497,297 for 2016 international-route mariners; the cited 2020 MSA report (Table 1-1) gives 497,197. Figure 3 also prints +7.94% for 2020 international-route growth; the report gives +3.0%, and the figure's own numbers (592,998 over 575,823) give +2.98%. The other checked entries in the figure match the official…; `CMR51-N154`: The sentence calls COSCO Shipping Seafarer Management the largest crew manning provider in China, managing 42,000 seafarers on over 1,300 vessels (with a note that the company's website claims to be the world's largest). 32 notes carry a reader note on how the note is displayed or cited.

paper_memo.memo_title: One-Page Analytical Memo — CMR-52: Everything Everywhere All At Once (Wang, Bernardo, Wu & Erickson, April 2026)

sections.heading: 1. Strategic Context & Core Thesis
sections.body: CMSI’s April 2026 report argues that the PLA’s 23–24 August 2025 ‘capstone’ amphibious exercise marks a shift from generic training to operationally grounded Taiwan rehearsal: it integrated many previously separate elements — floating causeway, beach and in-water obstacles, direct-to-beach LCT landings and over-the-horizon RORO launches — into one two-phase operation, and for the first time observed ran simultaneous landings at three locations spread about 360 km apart, roughly the length of Taiwan’s western coastline.

sections.heading: 2. Section-by-Section Analytical Breakdown
sections.body:
• Part 1 (pp. 1–4): Overview; the PLA’s growing use of dual-use civilian RORO ferries, deck cargo vessels and LCTs; Table 1 compares the 2025 exercise with 2021–2024 capstones.
• Part 2, Phase 1 (pp. 5–14): Honghai Bay, 23 August — six LCTs (four confirmed) and about 215 vehicles ashore; a ~365 m floating causeway (four ~70 × 9 m self-propelled segments and a 70 × 25 m barge); PU TUO DAO launching AFVs ~5 km offshore; two ferries unloading at Xiaomo Port.
• Part 2, Phase 2 (pp. 14–19): 24 August — four ROROs at Hougang, Qianhu and Houcai Bays, deployment distances of 1.5–6.2 km, synchronized formation sailing toward the Taiwan Strait median line.
• Part 3 (pp. 19–23): obstacles (aquaculture rafts, anti-landing barriers), ideal weather, and the 360 km geographic-scaling argument.

sections.heading: 3. Key Doctrinal Concepts, Terminology & Quantitative Claims
sections.body:
• Capstone exercise: the annual late-summer joint amphibious event; this one ran 23–24 August 2025.
• Landing methods: LCT direct-to-beach; floating causeway; pier offload (Xiaomo Port); RORO over-the-horizon AFV launch.
• Floating causeway lengths: 450 m (2021), 650 m (2022–2023), none in 2024, ~365 m (2025).
• RORO group: eight ROROs in August 2025 versus five in 2023; 163–190 m long, 25–26 m wide, roughly 2,000 troops and 300 vehicles per ship.
• Site separation: ~360 km farthest (Hougang Bay to Honghai Bay 245 km plus ~45 km to Xiaomo Port).

sections.heading: 4. Audit Assessment & Analytical Significance
sections.body:
Of the 5 reference rows in CMR-52, 4 are rated `ok` and 1 (`[CMR52-R05]`) is rated `fix`: Appendix A’s timeline contains chronological inversions and the AIS identifiers (MMSIs) for the HUA YI vessels are inconsistent between the footnotes and Appendix B. The report’s analytical claims rest on commercial imagery and AIS, which the authors qualify (for example, only four of six LCTs visually confirmed).

**Footnote rows**: all 101 footnotes were extracted and consolidated into 74 source rows in the Reference Audit Matrix (CMR52-N001 to CMR52-N101). Repeat citations of the same source within this paper, including Ibid. and short-form notes, share one row, which lists each note's passage and result. Footnote-level result: 101 notes: 10 (10%) are confirmed, 0 of them against a retrieved source and 10 after an outside web search (8 of the latter with a slip or an unchecked detail noted); 2 are flagged for reader check; 91 (90%) are not confirmed. Of the 91 notes not confirmed, 3 are Chinese-language sources that have not been searched in Chinese (a search in Chinese could settle some of them); 64 were judged not web-checkable (55 the authors' own data, imagery or analysis; 5 notes that are explanatory text or a fragment, not a citation; 4 other items); 24 were searched on the web without finding corroboration. A source row is `ok` only when every note in it is confirmed, and `fix` when a note is confirmed wrong; the paper's 74 source rows are 3 `ok`, 0 `fix` and 71 `unk`. Notes flagged for reader check, for example (the outside search found something a reader should look at; none is a finding that the author is wrong): `CMR52-N081`: The sentence says the North Group operated in three locations in Southern Fujian including the Gulei Peninsula and Hougang Bay, and the South Group in Honghai Bay; `CMR52-N094`: The sentence says that by 2024 the PLA had completed the exploratory phase of its training reforms and established new training models, citing Yang and Tang on Strait Thunder-2025A. The retrieved China Brief summary describes the drill as routine large-scale training signalling more drills and does not mention an exploratory…. 38 notes carry a reader note on how the note is displayed or cited.

rows.source: Conscription System, Twice-a-Year Cycle (2021) and Revised Conscription Regulations (2021, 2023) (pp. 2-8; Notes 1-34)
rows.usage: Documents the Military Service Law and 2021/2023 Regulations on Conscription, the 14-department joint conference (2020), the MND Recruiting Office, the 2021 move to twice-a-year conscription (spring 45 percent, fall 55 percent of the annual quota per an Anhui MD officer), conscription ages (Table 1), and National Defense Reserve Battalions (Jilin: 97 college reserve companies, 75 percent of college conscripts).
rows.finding: Supported by the cited Xinhua, PLA Daily, State Council and China Military Online items; the 45/55 split and Jilin figures rest on single Chinese-media sources. The authors state the college-student share of recruits rose from under 30 percent (2013) to over 80 percent (2023) 'according to one source' (p. 18).

rows.source: Physically Unfit Recruit Pool and Other Recruitment Challenges (>55% Failed Physicals at Longdong University; 56.9% in One City in 2017; 177 of 699 PLAN Recruits Overweight; pp. 21-25; Notes 96-106)
rows.usage: Reports overburdened PAFD cadres, university indifference (Henan Institute of Technology survey; Longdong University), and the fitness problem: more than 55 percent of Longdong students failing physicals over three years, 56.9 percent failing in one city (2017), lowered standards since 2014 for slightly overweight or imperfect-vision applicants, and a 2024 survey in which 177 of 699 PLAN recruits were overweight.
rows.finding: Supported by the cited Defense Industry Conversion in China, BBC, SCMP, China Military Online and Journal of Navy Medicine items; the figures are local or single-source examples, not national rates, and the report does not give a national 50-70 percent failure rate.

rows.source: PLAN Sergeant, Academy, Flight-Cadet and Officer Pipelines: Targeted Training (2.5 + 0.5 years), Direct Recruitment, Naval Academies, Flight Cadet Program (pp. 9-15; Notes 35-61)
rows.usage: Details the 2022 targeted-training sergeant program (48 vocational colleges, about 6,000 yuan a month on graduation, 12,000 yuan tuition reimbursement, male-to-female quota ratios of 33:1 to 82:1 in 2022 and 108:1 overall in 2024; Table 2), direct recruitment of sergeants (400+ specialties; up to 16,000/20,000 yuan reimbursement; five-year minimum), the five PLAN academies and NUDT, the PLAN Flight Cadet Program (established 2015; women accepted only in 2023), and direct recruitment of officers from top-tier universities.
rows.finding: Supported by the cited Baidu, Zhongshan, The Paper, NetEase, China Military Online and CHSI sources, with PLAN-specific details of Table 2 drawn from college admission brochures. The report does not describe dual-degree pilot tracks at named Beijing universities.

rows.usage: Compares 2024 military pay (junior sergeant 5,500+ to 7,500+ yuan, ~$766-$1,044 at 7.1812 RMB/USD; conscripts 1,000+) with Salary Explorer civilian averages (factory worker 8,370; mechanic 11,500; computer programmer '28,3000' ~$3,941; GN&C engineer 31,666 yuan a month), and notes the college share of recruits rose from under 30 percent (2013) to over 80 percent (2023).
rows.finding: Supported on the USD conversion ($3,941 x 7.1812 = 28,301 yuan), with a one-zero typographical slip in '28,3000 yuan/month' for 28,300. The wage comparison is, in the authors' words, 'very rough' and rests on Salary Explorer. Rated ok under the house slip rule.

rows.source: Military-service tuition assistance: RMB 16,000 and RMB 20,000 caps
rows.usage: Note 48 reports these annual tuition-compensation and loan-repayment caps for directly recruited sergeants.
rows.finding:
**Open-claim evidence follow-up, November 22, 2026 — Correction established.** Resolved to a dated-policy correction. The report, published May 20, 2026, presents RMB16,000/20,000 as the direct-recruit sergeant tuition-compensation and loan-repayment ceilings (PDF p. 14, note 48). The National Student Financial Assistance Management Center's October 17, 2024 implementation notice, preserved by Jilin University, expressly includes direct-recruit sergeants and uses the enlistment-notice date to distinguish cohorts: RMB16,000/20,000 for September 1, 2023–August 31, 2024, and RMB20,000/25,000 from September 1, 2024. Finance Ministry notice 财教〔2024〕188号 subsequently confirms the new general service-assistance ceilings. The earlier pair is valid for its specified cohort; the unqualified 2026 statement requires a cohort/date qualification or the updated ceilings. paper_memo.memo_title: One-Page Analytical Memo — CMR-53: PLA Navy Recruiting (Erin Richter & Joshua Arostegui, May 20, 2026)

sections.heading: 1. Strategic Context & Core Thesis
sections.body: China Maritime Report No. 53 (May 2026) by Erin Richter and Joshua Arostegui outlines how the PLAN recruits within China's national military service system. Its thesis: most PLAN manpower comes through centrally managed conscription, supplemented by the navy's own recruitment of sergeants, officers, civilians and flight cadets; the PLA is moving to precision recruitment and a much more college-educated intake, yet qualitative problems (stretched local recruiters, weak university support, poor fitness, low pay relative to civilian tech jobs) persist.

sections.heading: 2. Structure & Evidence
sections.body:
• Service system and cycle (pp. 2-8): Military Service Law; conscripts versus sergeants; 2021 and 2023 conscription regulations; 14-department joint conference; twice-a-year conscription since 2021 (spring 45 percent, fall 55 percent).
• Accession paths (pp. 7-15): National Defense Reserve Battalions; targeted training of sergeants (2022; 2.5 years at 48 vocational colleges plus six months); direct sergeant recruitment (400+ specialties); five PLAN academies; Flight Cadet Program (2015); direct officer recruitment.
• Outreach and incentives (pp. 15-21): precision recruitment, propaganda, pay (Table 3), entitlements, retirement benefits.
• Challenges and conclusion (pp. 21-25): overburdened PAFD cadres, university indifference, a physically unfit pool; the PLAN meets quantitative goals but struggles to attract top STEM students.

sections.heading: 3. Key Quantities
sections.body:
• College-student share of recruits: under 30 percent (2013) to over 80 percent (2023), per one source.
• Pay (2024): junior sergeants 5,500-7,500+ yuan a month (~$766-$1,044); factory worker 8,370; mechanic 11,500; programmer 28,300 (printed '28,3000'); GN&C engineer 31,666.
• Fitness: over 55 percent failing at Longdong University; 56.9 percent in one city (2017); 177 of 699 PLAN recruits overweight (2024 survey).
• Targeted-training quotas: male-to-female 33:1 to 82:1 (2022), 108:1 overall (2024).

sections.heading: 4. Audit Assessment
sections.body:
All four reference rows are rated ok. The only logged defect is the '28,3000' digit slip on p. 19. Fitness and wage figures are local or single-source examples and are not presented by the authors as national rates.

**Footnote rows**: all 106 footnotes were extracted and consolidated into 70 source rows in the Reference Audit Matrix (CMR53-N001 to CMR53-N106). Repeat citations of the same source within this paper, including Ibid. and short-form notes, share one row, which lists each note's passage and result. Footnote-level result: 106 notes: 24 (23%) are confirmed, 2 of them against a retrieved source and 22 after an outside web search (20 of the latter with a slip or an unchecked detail noted); 1 is flagged for reader check; 82 (77%) are not confirmed. Of the 82 notes not confirmed, 42 are Chinese-language sources that have not been searched in Chinese (a search in Chinese could settle some of them); 2 were judged not web-checkable (1 note that is a fragment or run-on text attached to a Chinese-language source; 1 note that is explanatory text or a fragment, not a citation); 37 were searched on the web without finding corroboration; 1 has not been searched. A source row is `ok` only when every note in it is confirmed, and `fix` when a note is confirmed wrong; the paper's 70 source rows are 14 `ok`, 0 `fix` and 56 `unk`. Notes flagged for reader check, for example (the outside search found something a reader should look at; none is a finding that the author is wrong): `CMR53-N048`: The sentence says directly recruited sergeants get tuition reimbursement and loan repayment up to 16,000 yuan (undergraduate) and 20,000 yuan (graduate). Sources found give PLA tuition compensation as 6,000 yuan per year (2011) or up to 24,000 yuan (undated Shanghai report), while 16,000 and 20,000 yuan appear as civilian…. 16 notes carry a reader note on how the note is displayed or cited.

sections.heading: 1. Strategic Context & Core Thesis
sections.body: China Maritime Report No. 54 (2 June 2026) by CMSI's Ryan D. Martinson, drawing mainly on PLA Daily, People's Navy, Qiushi and Xinhua sources, argues that Xi Jinping has been a decisive, personally engaged driver of the PLAN's transformation, and should be seen as the PRC's first 'navalist' leader. The credit for execution goes to the service, but political interest and support were the precondition.

sections.heading: 2. Structure & Evidence
sections.body:
• Introduction and engagement table (pp. 2-5): opens with the 8 December 2012 voyage on the destroyer Haikou and lists 15 known engagements with the PLAN through the 5 November 2025 Fujian commissioning.
• 'Chairman Xi's Actions' (pp. 6-13): the 2014 Military Strategic Guidelines update that singled out maritime struggle; Xi's reported personal decisions on SSBNs, carriers and the Djibouti base; shifts in PLAN operating areas; the 2015-17 reforms (Leading Small Group created March 2014; PLANMC from 2 to 8 brigades); and the Paracel/Spratly build-out.
• 'Chairman Xi's Ideas' (pp. 13-19): the 30 July 2013 Politburo speech, the 2004 Zhejiang Daily interview, the 'four shifts', weiquan versus weiwen, and the 'three at-seas' (Note 86: unattributed in the 2013 Science of Military Strategy, p. 209).

sections.heading: 3. Key Claims & Quantities
sections.body:
• 15 known engagements, December 2012-November 2025 (the list is incomplete; an April 2016 article counts six inspections by then).
• Fleet reviews: 12 April 2018 (South China Sea; 48 vessels, 76 aircraft, 10,000+ personnel) and 23 April 2019 (Qingdao).
• Force structure: PLANMC two to eight brigades; nearly two dozen Type 056 corvettes transferred to the China Coast Guard in 2022; fighter, bomber and air-defense units moved to the PLAAF in 2023.
• Formulations: 'Strong countries are strong at sea, while weak countries are weak at sea'; 'three at-seas'; 'world-class navy' (24 May 2017 PLAN HQ speech).

sections.heading: 4. Audit Assessment
sections.body:
All four reference rows are rated ok. The only logged defect is the Note 80 date slip ('11 September 11, 2015'). Several attributions of personal decisions to Xi rest on PLAN and Party-press statements that the report itself treats as 'apparent' or 'purported', so they are best read as official narrative rather than independently confirmed history.

**Footnote rows**: all 92 footnotes were extracted and consolidated into 76 source rows in the Reference Audit Matrix (CMR54-N001 to CMR54-N092). Footnote-level result: 92 notes: 30 (33%) are confirmed, 9 of them against a retrieved source and 21 after an outside web search (15 of the latter with a slip or an unchecked detail noted); 62 (67%) are not confirmed. Of the 62 notes not confirmed, 35 are Chinese-language sources that have not been searched in Chinese (a search in Chinese could settle some of them); 4 were judged not web-checkable (1 the authors' own data, imagery or analysis; 3 notes that are explanatory text or a fragment, not a citation); 23 were searched on the web without finding corroboration. paper_memo.memo_title: One-Page Analytical Memo — CMR-55: Loading the Well Deck: The PLA Navy's Maturing Role in Projecting Joint Ground Forces (Joshua Arostegui, June 24, 2026)

sections.heading: 1. Strategic Context & Core Thesis
sections.body: China Maritime Report No. 55 (June 2026) by Joshua Arostegui of the U.S. Army War College's China Landpower Studies Center argues that since 2023 the PLA has run an annual rhythm of loading PLA Army combat, engineering and support units onto PLAN amphibious ships for overseas exercises. The report reads this as evidence that the post-2016 joint structure works and that China's overseas power-projection ceiling is not set by the PLAN Marine Corps, which it calls a relatively light force.

sections.heading: 2. Section-by-Section Breakdown
sections.body:
• Introduction and 'The Army's Dilemma' (pp. 1-3): pre-reform silos; Blue Strike 2016 carried only organic PLAN marines; the PLAA's organic strategic lift is insufficient for overseas action, so it relies on PLAN lift.
• Cambodia 2023-2024 (pp. 3-10): Jinggangshan (999) carried CSK181 and support vehicles about 1,300 nm for Golden Dragon-2023 (20 March-8 April; about 3,000 troops); Qilianshan (985) carried PLZ10 combination guns and CSK181s for Golden Dragon-2024 (16-30 May), with RAdm Gao Xiucheng as the first naval exercise commander.
• 2025 on both sides of the Malacca Strait (pp. 11-17): Golden Dragon-2025 (14-28 May) used Changbaishan (989) to land ZBD04A IFVs, CSK181s, PCL171 howitzers and a radar detachment at Ream; Peace and Friendship-2025 (15-23 October) sent Jinggangshan with Yinchuan and Jingmen to Port Klang.
• Tanzania (pp. 17-19): Peace and Unity-2024 moved a battalion-sized force on Qilianshan and Wuzhishan with Hefei escort and Y-20 airlift; the largest force sent abroad for an exercise that did not require rail transport.
• 'What the PLAN Gains', four U.S.-planner implications and the Conclusion (pp. 19-22).

sections.heading: 3. Key Claims & Quantities
sections.body:
• Order of battle by exercise: 2023 about 3,000 troops both sides; 2024 more than 2,000 personnel (760 PLA); 2025 845 PLA and more than 1,300 Cambodian; Peace and Friendship-2025 more than 700 PLA personnel.
• Command pattern: a PLAN officer commanded in 2024 (RAdm Gao); a PLAAF major general in 2025 (Lu Guangkun); a PLAA major general in Malaysia (Dai Bin); the STC deputy commander was senior VIP at three straight Golden Dragon closings.
• Concept: 'access without basing' using civilian ports (Sihanoukville, Ream, Port Klang), per Note 50 and the 2013 Science of Military Strategy and RAND.

sections.heading: 4. Audit Assessment
sections.body:
All four reference rows are rated ok. The only defects are cosmetic footnote slips: Note 11 ('3 March 2022' for a 20230322 clip), Note 35 ('March 13, 2025' for a May 2025 article), duplicated 'www.sohu.com/a/' strings in Notes 29 and 59, and two stray punctuation marks in Notes 38 and 57. Headline figures follow the cited state-media and MND reports; the personnel splits could not be independently confirmed outside those sources.

**Footnote rows**: all 65 footnotes were extracted and consolidated into 56 source rows in the Reference Audit Matrix (CMR55-N001 to CMR55-N065). Repeat citations of the same source within this paper, including Ibid. and short-form notes, share one row, which lists each note's passage and result. Footnote-level result: 65 notes: 17 (26%) are confirmed, 6 of them against a retrieved source and 11 after an outside web search (11 of the latter with a slip or an unchecked detail noted); 1 is flagged for reader check; 48 (74%) are not confirmed. Of the 48 notes not confirmed, 13 are Chinese-language sources that have not been searched in Chinese (a search in Chinese could settle some of them); 10 were judged not web-checkable (1 note that is a fragment or run-on text attached to a Chinese-language source; 8 notes that are explanatory text or a fragment, not a citation; 1 other item); 24 were searched on the web without finding corroboration; 1 has not been searched. A source row is `ok` only when every note in it is confirmed, and `fix` when a note is confirmed wrong; the paper's 56 source rows are 15 `ok`, 0 `fix` and 41 `unk`. Notes flagged for reader check, for example (the outside search found something a reader should look at; none is a finding that the author is wrong): `CMR55-N035`: The sentence is a photo caption (embarked soldiers rehearsing onboard emergency management while transiting to Cambodia for Golden Dragon-2025). The note dates the PLA Daily / mod.gov.cn item 13 March 2025, but Chinese-language reposts (Global Times, via CCTV Military) report the force arriving at Ream on 12 May 2025 and the…. 3 notes carry a reader note on how the note is displayed or cited.

rows.source: PLAN Share of Senior PLA Positions and CMC Representation, 2015-2025 (Exhibits 1-2, pp. 3-5; Notes 7-13)

Exhibit 1 is a chart whose values could not be read from the text extraction.

rows.usage: States that the PLAN share of CMC department directors and deputy directors was 7 percent in 2024 (6 percent in 2016), that 13 naval officers held such posts in 2016-2024, that Miao Hua, Wang Renhua (2019-2025) and Guan Youfei (2016-2017) were the three top-job exceptions, and that naval officers served in the Joint Staff Department (Sun Jianguo, Jiang Guoping) and as theater commander (Yuan Yubai, 2017-2021) and political commissar (Liu Qingsong, Eastern Theater since 2023).
rows.finding: Supported by the cited DoD directories, Gunnell's People's Liberation Army as Organization 3.0 and CNR reporting; Note 17 adds that Liu Qingsong started in the air force and transferred to the navy in 2018. Exhibit 2 is a chart whose values could not be read.

rows.usage: Tabulates PLAN commanders (Hu Zhongming from December 2023; Dong Jun September 2021-December 2023; Shen Jinlong 2017-2021; Wu Shengli 2006-2016; Zhang Dingfa 2003-2006), political commissars (Yuan Huazhi, Qin Shengxiang, Miao Hua, Liu Xiaojiang, Hu Yanlin) and four CMC alumni (Jiang Guoping, Wang Dazhong, Li Hanjun, Ma Lixin), and concludes that joint service is not a normal career path to the top of the PLAN.
rows.finding: Supported on the table contents and the text's inferences (two of five commanders held senior CMC roles; no career PLAN political officer reached the top commissar post via the CMC; Li Hanjun was removed in 2025 per CMSI Note #15). Exhibit 4's second column header reads 'Dates as PLAN Commander' instead of political commissar. Rated ok under the house slip rule.

rows.source: Impact of CMC Policies: Command and Control, Recruitment and Training, Manning and Mobilization, Forces and Capabilities (pp. 10-16; Notes 26-62)
rows.usage: Describes concessions the navy accepted: theater commanders gaining operational control, direct recruitment of STEM graduates (2025 notice: under 24 for undergraduates, under 29 for master's, under 34 for PhDs), academy downsizing from 67 to 37, the 2022 Reservist Law, the 2023 transfer of shore-based aviation (H-6J, JH-7) to the PLAAF, the transfer of 20 Type 056 corvettes to the CCG, and Marine Corps growth to '11' brigades; the Conclusion cites 216 surface combatants in 2004 and 332 in 2023.
rows.finding: Supported by the cited DoD, CASI, CRS, Xinhua and Zhihu/QQ sources. Cross-paper discrepancy: the 11-brigade Marine Corps figure (Note 59) conflicts with CMR-54's eight brigades and with the text's own 2 + 3 + 3 arithmetic. Logged as a note, not a fix; the row stays ok because the main claims do not depend on it.

rows.source: Liu Huaqing’s Party commission vice-chairmanship began in 1989
rows.usage: Paraphrase of original passage. CMR-56, PDF p. 5, leadership history and note 6. The report gives 1989–97 for Liu’s vice-chairmanship.

Use those dates for the Party commission. The state commission followed its separate appointment timetable.
evidence: Official biographical article on Liu Huaqing

rows.usage: Paraphrase of original passage. CMR-56, PDF p. 7, history of the commission’s reorganization. The report says the former general departments were replaced by 15 functional agencies.
rows.finding: The published March 2016 Ministry of National Defense briefing identifies four former headquarters and 15 new agencies, including departments, commissions and offices. The official count documents the reform structure. The later personnel ratios in the report use a separate data source.
evidence: Chinese defense ministry’s restructuring briefing, Xinhua transcript

rows.source: The U.S. joint-duty rule cited by the report applies to combatant command
rows.usage: Paraphrase of original passage. CMR-56, PDF p. 8, comparison with the U.S. personnel system and note 18. The report refers to joint duty as a U.S. prerequisite for command under Goldwater–Nichols.
rows.finding: The 1986 law and 10 U.S.C. §164 connect joint duty to eligibility for assignment as a combatant commander. The statute includes waiver authority. The formulation should be read within that statutory scope, with different rules applying to other commands.
evidence: Office of the Law Revision Counsel, 10 U.S.C. §164

rows.source: China’s Reservist Law was adopted in 2022 and took effect in 2023
rows.usage: Paraphrase of original passage. CMR-56, PDF p. 16, reservist legislation and note 52. The report identifies the Reservist Law by its 2022 adoption year.
rows.finding: The National People’s Congress gazette prints the adoption on December 30, 2022 and implementation from March 1, 2023. The contemporaneous news story on December 31 reports the preceding legislative action. Keep the adoption, reporting and effective dates distinct.
evidence: NPC Standing Committee Gazette, adopted law and effective date

rows.source: The academy reduction refers to the 2017 institution count
rows.usage: Paraphrase of original passage. CMR-56, PDF p. 14, discussion of changes to the institution network. The report gives a reduction from 67 to 37 military academic institutions.
rows.finding: Independent institutional studies from CASI and Japan’s National Institute for Defense Studies give the changes as part of the 2017 reform. The numbers count institutions under the study definitions. They do not measure seats, training quality or annual graduation volumes.

paper_memo.memo_title: One-Page Analytical Memo — CMR-56: The Silent Service: Assessing PLAN Influence in the Central Military Commission (Natalie Shen & Joel Wuthnow, July 15, 2026)

sections.heading: 1. Strategic Context & Core Thesis
sections.body: China Maritime Report No. 56 (July 2026) by Natalie Shen and NDU's Joel Wuthnow asks whether the PLAN's growth has given it commensurate bureaucratic influence. The answer is no: the navy is a 'decision-taker' whose growth was driven top-down by Hu Jintao and Xi Jinping, with only modest representation on the CMC and in its departments and career incentives that steer rising naval officers away from joint staff jobs.

sections.heading: 2. Evidence & Structure
sections.body:
• Senior-leadership data (pp. 3-6): PLAN share of senior billets 12 percent (2015), 13 percent (2016), 16 percent (2024); army 54 percent, air force 19 percent, Rocket Force 6 percent in 2024; one PLAN officer on the CMC in 2016-2024 and none as of 2025; 7 percent of CMC department directors and deputies in 2024.
• Career patterns (pp. 6-9): Exhibits 3-5 on PLAN commanders, commissars and CMC alumni; joint experience is not a prerequisite for advancement and many commissars were career army officers.
• Impact of CMC policies (pp. 10-15): loss of operational control to theater commanders; direct commissioning of STEM graduates; reserve reforms; 2023 aviation transfer to the PLAAF; 20 Type 056 corvettes to the CCG; Marine Corps expansion.
• Conclusion (pp. 16-17): the navy grew from 216 to 332 surface combatants (2004-2023) but cannot lobby effectively; the army kept top management roles.

sections.heading: 3. Key Quantities & Concepts
sections.body:
• 22/182 (2015), 24/192 (2016), 21/131 (2024) PLAN senior billets; 13 naval officers in CMC department leadership posts in 2016-2024; navy manpower share 12 percent (army 47, air force 20).
• Exhibit 3 and 4 tenures: Hu Zhongming from December 2023, Dong Jun 2021-2023, Shen Jinlong 2017-2021, Wu Shengli 2006-2016; Yuan Huazhi January 2022-2024/5.
• Concept: 'decision-taker' versus 'decision-maker'.

sections.heading: 4. Audit Assessment
sections.body:
All four reference rows are rated ok. Logged defects: the Exhibit 4 column header slip (p. 8), a stray '=limits' (p. 17), and a cross-paper discrepancy over the number of Marine Corps brigades (11 here versus eight in CMR-54). Exhibits 1 and 2 are charts whose values could not be checked from text.

**Footnote rows**: all 69 footnotes were extracted and consolidated into 61 source rows in the Reference Audit Matrix (CMR56-N001 to CMR56-N069). Repeat citations of the same source within this paper, including Ibid. and short-form notes, share one row, which lists each note's passage and result. Footnote-level result: 69 notes: 25 (36%) are confirmed, 3 of them against a retrieved source and 22 after an outside web search (19 of the latter with a slip or an unchecked detail noted); 1 is flagged for reader check; 44 (64%) are not confirmed. Of the 44 notes not confirmed, 13 are Chinese-language sources that have not been searched in Chinese (a search in Chinese could settle some of them); 1 was judged not web-checkable (1 the authors' own data, imagery or analysis); 30 were searched on the web without finding corroboration. A source row is `ok` only when every note in it is confirmed, and `fix` when a note is confirmed wrong; the paper's 61 source rows are 22 `ok`, 0 `fix` and 39 `unk`. Notes flagged for reader check, for example (the outside search found something a reader should look at; none is a finding that the author is wrong): `CMR56-N058`: The sentence says the Army transferred three amphibious brigades to the PLANMC in 2017. Reports found describe the former 77th Brigade (26th Group Army) as transferred from the Army, with three further brigades from coastal defense forces and two original Marine brigades by December 2017; Jamestown estimates over 20,000…. 15 notes carry a reader note on how the note is displayed or cited.

rows.source: Party Committee Structure, First NPSC (1950-1953) and Current NPSC Membership (pp. 2-5; Notes 1-14)
rows.usage: Explains the Party Congress/Committee/Standing Committee hierarchy (Navy Party Congress every five years; 12th in May 2017, 13th in June 2022; Party Committee of about 50; Discipline Inspection Committee of about 10), the first provisional Party committee (June 1950) and first Standing Committee (1953) under Xiao Jinguang, and the likely 12-member current NPSC (Leng Shaojie as acting commissar and Secretary after Yuan Huazhi's October 2025 expulsion; Hu Zhongming as Deputy Secretary; Chief of Staff unidentified after Li Hanjun's June 2025 dismissal).
rows.finding: Supported by the cited Organization Department history, People's Navy, Xinhua, Nikkei and BBC items; the report openly flags that the Chief of Staff is unidentified and that NPSC membership is inferred ('likely consists of 12 members').

rows.source: Table 1 (NPSC Members, Nov 2025), Table 2 (Retirement Ages) and the Cohort Comparison: Age, Tenure, Experience (pp. 5-9; Notes 15-24)
rows.usage: Reports a cohort aged about 58-63 (average just under 60.8, median 61, against 61.5 at the end of the Hu era), average tenure of 2.8 years versus 4.5 in 2013, retirement ages by grade (65/63/55 with extension), career backgrounds (Hu Zhongming 2002 circumnavigation and first Jin-class SSBN; Li Yujie as Qingdao CO; Wang Hongli on the 23rd escort task force) and the ground-force origin of all four political officers.
rows.finding: Supported by the cited People's Navy, Global Times, Caixin and Law on Officers in Active Service sources; two birth dates are unknown (Note 16) so the average rests on ten members. Rank slip on p. 6: 'ADM Leng Shaojie' versus VADM in Table 1 and p. 4. Rated ok under the house slip rule.

rows.source: NPSC Political Authorities: Ten Prohibitions, Political-Legal Commission, Inspection Leading Group, Theory Study Central Group, Thematic Education (pp. 10-15; Notes 25-58)
rows.usage: Documents the Party-control bodies: Ten Prohibitions (December 2015), Rules on the Work of the Navy Party Committee, the PLAN Political and Legal Affairs Commission (first plenary 20 July 2016; Ding Haichun as secretary), the Leading Group for Inspection Work (four teams by 2022; 2023 rounds), the Theory Study Central Group (first session April 2018, monthly), and the thematic-education leading group (April 2023; second meeting 30 June 2023).
rows.finding: Supported by the cited PLA Daily, People's Navy, Xinhua and CCP regulation sources. Note 41 is dated 2010 against a text date of about 2016 for the inspection group, and the authors state they could not find the thematic-education group's founding notice (Note 57). Rated ok.

rows.source: NPSC in Man, Train and Equip Activities and the Conclusion's Outlook (pp. 16-20; Notes 59-74)
rows.usage: Covers the 2018 single-ship command regulations, 2021 Regulations on Naval Vessels (Trial), the September 2022 talent work meeting (Dong Jun, Yuan Huazhi), the Training Bureau and Political Work Department personnel bureaus (Liu Bencheng), equipment/logistics reform under Party Committee direction (Zhou Xuming at the 29-30 October 2020 Zhoushan meeting), and the forecast of more joint, overseas and strategic experience (7 of 11 known members have held a joint billet, per Note 70).
rows.finding: Supported by the cited PLA Daily and People's Navy items and DoD, Wuthnow and Erickson/Strange sources. Slip on p. 17: 'PBSC member VADM Liu Bencheng' for NPSC. Note 59's 2019 source date versus the text's 2018 regulation is a minor wrinkle. Rated ok under the house slip rule.

rows.source: Political and Legal Affairs Commission oversight: the cited CRS description
rows.usage: Paraphrase of extracted passage, CMR57-N034: The central commission oversees the courts, procuratorate and ministries of public security, state security and justice.
rows.finding: Reviewed November 11, 2026. The January 3, 2025 version of CRS IF12505 explicitly names all five institutions in its commission description and notes their heads’ membership. The citation date and author also match. This verifies the cited institutional description as of that edition, not every practical dimension of the commission’s influence.
evidence: CRS IF12505, January 3, 2025, CPC functional departments

rows.source: Party standing committees and the asserted four plenums per year
rows.usage: Paraphrase of extracted passage, CMR57-N005: The full Party committee meets periodically, often four times yearly, while its standing committee serves as the highest executive body.
rows.finding:
**Open-claim evidence follow-up, November 22, 2026 — Reviewed; unresolved.** The supplied passage says full committees often meet four times yearly. The Party Constitution provisions for local committees establish a minimum for a different organizational category, not the observed frequency of the PLAN-level body. A standing committee’s executive role does not itself establish how often the full committee meets. No organization-specific four-meeting record was recovered here.

**Remaining gap or scope limit.** The relevant military Party rule or a dated series of full-committee plenums at the level discussed.

**Earlier audit record (preserved).** Reviewed November 11, 2026. The 2022 CPC Constitution supports collective leadership (Article 10) and standing committees acting between local committee plenums (Article 28). Article 27 sets a minimum of two local committee plenums yearly, not four; that minimum does not disprove more frequent meetings. Article 24 assigns armed-forces Party organization to CMC rules. Neither the typical four-per-year frequency nor the Navy-specific application is established by these provisions. The cited Lieberthal and McGregor book passages were not retrieved. Consistency review, November 14, 2026. The constitution's local-committee minimum and its separate armed-forces provision concern distinct scopes. As in CMS04-R08, a Party-wide rule cannot establish the figures for a particular institutional population. Four per year still needs the cited usage account or dated meeting records. Follow-up review, November 14, 2026. The Party constitution distinguishes rules for local committees and service-specific rules for armed forces Party organization. The recent CMR57-R07 and R08 audits establish amendment and campaign dates only. Confirm a typical four annual plenums with dated records for the relevant level. Follow-up review, November 15, 2026. The constitution’s two-meeting floor governs local Party committees and is not evidence of observed meeting frequency in the organization described. A dated organization-specific rule or meeting record is needed to establish the four-meeting description.

claim_review.original_source: Party standing committees and the asserted four plenums per year
claim_review.original_usage: Paraphrase of extracted passage, CMR57-N005: The full Party committee meets periodically, often four times yearly, while its standing committee serves as the highest executive body.
claim_review.remaining_gap: The relevant military Party rule or a dated series of full-committee plenums at the level discussed.

rows.source: The report places incorporation of Xi Jinping Thought in the Party constitution in November 2017 and in the state constitution in March 2018.
rows.usage: Paraphrase of original passage. CMR57-N049, sentence on Party and state constitutional dates. The report places incorporation of Xi Jinping Thought in the Party constitution in November 2017 and in the state constitution in March 2018.
rows.finding: Reviewed November 14, 2026. The Nineteenth Party Congress adopted the Party constitutional amendment on October 24, 2017. The state amendment is dated March 11, 2018. Correct the first date. The separate claim about when a particular institution implemented study arrangements requires its own evidence.

rows.source: The Party-wide campaign ran from April 2023 to February 2024 and had stated ideological education aims.
rows.usage: Paraphrase of original passage. CMR57-N055 and CMR57-N056, paragraph on the Party-wide thematic campaign. The Party-wide campaign ran from April 2023 to February 2024 and had stated ideological education aims.
rows.finding: Reviewed November 14, 2026. The Party’s April 2023 fact sheet documents the launch and objectives. The February 4, 2024 Xinhua report records a wrap-up meeting. Those establish the public campaign milestones. Local implementation dates are a separate question.

rows.source: The report calls Xi Jinping General Secretary of the Politburo Standing Committee.
rows.usage: Paraphrase of original passage. CMR-57, PDF p. 4, paragraph on Party standing committees and note 8. The report calls Xi Jinping General Secretary of the Politburo Standing Committee.
rows.finding: Reviewed November 15, 2026. The 20th Central Committee’s first plenum separately elected members of the Politburo Standing Committee and the General Secretary of the Central Committee. It also selected Xi as chairman of the Party CMC. The report conflates the office title with membership of the Standing Committee.
evidence: Organizational Work Regulations cited in note 8

rows.source: The 12th Navy Party Congress convened in May 2017, several months before the 19th national Party Congress.
rows.usage: Paraphrase of original passage. CMR-57, PDF p. 4, note 3. The 12th Navy Party Congress convened in May 2017, several months before the 19th national Party Congress.
rows.finding: Reviewed November 15, 2026. Contemporaneous Xinhua reporting places the Navy delegates in Beijing on 24 May. The 19th national Congress opened in October. The two congress numbers refer to separate institutional sequences.
evidence: Xinhua, 24 May 2017 meeting, via People’s Daily
Party Constitution adopted by the national Congress on 24 October 2017

rows.source: The Navy Party Committee recently comprised around 50 officers and its discipline commission around 10 members.
rows.usage: Paraphrase of original passage. CMR-57, PDF p. 4, paragraph on the Navy Congress, notes 3–4. The Navy Party Committee recently comprised around 50 officers and its discipline commission around 10 members.
rows.finding:
**Open-claim evidence follow-up, November 22, 2026 — Reviewed; unresolved.** The 2017 official report and the naval-journal account verify the congress and election of party/discipline bodies. paper_memo.memo_title: One-Page Analytical Memo — CMR-57: Sailing Thousands of Miles Without Losing Course: The Roles and Authorities of the PLAN Party Standing Committee (Jeffrey Becker & Brian Waidelich, Aug 6, 2026)

sections.heading: 1. Strategic Context & Core Thesis
sections.body: China Maritime Report No. 57 (6 August 2026) by CNA's Jeffrey Becker and Brian Waidelich studies the PLAN Party Standing Committee (NPSC), the CCP's highest authority inside the navy. Its thesis is that the NPSC combines two functions, political control (loyalty to Xi Jinping as the Party's core) and administrative direction of personnel, training, procurement, logistics, finance and readiness, and that shorter tenures plus the navy's loss of a CMC seat have reduced the committee's influence even as its members' operational experience has widened.

sections.heading: 2. Structure & Evidence
sections.body:
• Party-structure background (pp. 2-4): Navy Party Congress every five years (12th May 2017; 13th June 2022); first provisional Party committee June 1950 and first Standing Committee 1953 under Xiao Jinguang.
• The current NPSC (pp. 4-9): likely 12 members as of January 2026; Leng Shaojie (acting commissar and Secretary) and Hu Zhongming (Deputy Secretary); ages 58-63 (average just under 60.8); average tenure 2.8 years versus 4.5 in 2013; all four political officers are career ground-force officers.
• Party-control tools and bodies (pp. 9-15): dual-hatting, personnel control and inspection; Ten Prohibitions (December 2015), Political and Legal Affairs Commission (July 2016), Inspection Leading Group (four teams by 2022), Theory Study Central Group (from April 2018), thematic education (April 2023).
• Man, train and equip (pp. 16-18) and Conclusion (pp. 18-20): regulations, talent work, Training Bureau, Political Work Department and equipment reform; future members likely to have more joint, overseas and strategic experience.

sections.heading: 3. Key Claims & Quantities
sections.body:
• 12 likely members; 11 known; 7 of the 11 have held a joint billet in the past decade (Note 70).
• Age average just under 60.8 and median 61 (two birth dates unknown), versus 61.5 at the end of the Hu era; retirement ages 65 (theater leader), 63 (theater deputy leader), 55 extendable by five years (corps leader).
• Tenure: about 2.8 years now versus 4.5 in 2013 (Wu Shengli 11 years as commander; Liu Xiaojiang 6 as commissar).
• NPSC-led bodies meet at least monthly; the Theory Study Central Group meets monthly.

sections.heading: 4. Audit Assessment
sections.body:
All four reference rows are rated ok. Logged slips are cosmetic: 'ADM Leng Shaojie' on p. 6 versus VADM and acting commissar in Table 1 and p. 4, and 'PBSC member VADM Liu Bencheng' on p. 17 for NPSC. The report is candid about gaps: the Chief of Staff is unidentified, two birth dates are unknown, and the founding of the thematic-education group could not be sourced, so membership counts and averages are estimates.

**Footnote rows**: all 74 footnotes were extracted and consolidated into 68 source rows in the Reference Audit Matrix (CMR57-N001 to CMR57-N073). Repeat citations of the same source within this paper, including Ibid. and short-form notes, share one row, which lists each note's passage and result. Footnote-level result: 74 notes: 18 (24%) are confirmed, 3 of them against a retrieved source and 15 after an outside web search (13 of the latter with a slip or an unchecked detail noted); 56 (76%) are not confirmed. Of the 56 notes not confirmed, 28 are Chinese-language sources that have not been searched in Chinese (a search in Chinese could settle some of them); 4 were judged not web-checkable (1 the authors' own data, imagery or analysis; 2 notes that are explanatory text or a fragment, not a citation; 1 other item); 24 were searched on the web without finding corroboration. A source row is `ok` only when every note in it is confirmed, and `fix` when a note is confirmed wrong; the paper's 68 source rows are 16 `ok`, 0 `fix` and 52 `unk`. 10 notes carry a reader note on how the note is displayed or cited.

rows.finding: The official January 9 report identifies the speaker, plenum and theme of strict Party governance. The separate Navy political-legal meeting in the note has a different date and would need its own documentation for branch-level implementation.
evidence: Supreme People’s Procuratorate republication of the January 9 speech report

rows.source: Legal interpretation of the RMB 30,000 threshold
rows.usage: Paraphrase of original passage. CMR-58, PDF p. 7, paragraph introducing referral to judicial bodies, note 17. The report presents RMB 30,000 as a categorical transfer threshold.
rows.finding: The 2016 judicial interpretation uses RMB 30,000 as the ordinary starting point for one criminal amount category and provides for specified circumstances at lower amounts. The underlying newspaper item was unavailable. The general criminal threshold does not independently establish the internal transfer procedure.
evidence: Supreme People’s Procuratorate copy of the judicial interpretation

rows.source: Publication and commencement of the 2025 discipline regulations
rows.usage: Paraphrase of original passage. CMR-58, PDF p. 15, paragraph following Figure 3. The report says the revised rules were issued in February and took effect in April 2025.
rows.finding: The defense ministry release reports the promulgation of the three revised regulations in February and specifies commencement on April 1, 2025. This verifies the rule dates separately from the figure’s source for procedural details.
evidence: Defense ministry notice of promulgation and commencement

rows.source: Starting point of the reported 45-day decision period
rows.usage: Paraphrase of original passage. CMR-58, PDF pp. 14–15, paragraph immediately before Figure 3, notes 56 and 58. The author describes a 45-day decision period starting from discovery.
rows.finding: The older translation cited for the figure and the official promulgation notice do not establish the trigger for the period in the revised text. The defense ministry’s chapter page timed out. Locate the applicable 2025 article and distinguish discovery, formal receipt and any extension. Source recheck. Article 130 of the retrieved 2025 regulation gives the ordinary period as 45 days measured from discovery of a disciplinary violation. It provides for extension subject to approval in complex or special cases. The article confirms the study’s starting point and identifies the period as the usual rule.

rows.source: June 2024 Yan’an political-work conference in the source notes
rows.usage: Paraphrase of original passage. CMR-58, PDF pp. 9–10, notes 33 and 35, referenced television report. The source identifies a military political-work conference held in Yan’an in June 2024.
rows.finding: CCTV’s program record and the Justice Ministry’s republication place the event in Yan’an and identify the June 2024 meeting. This confirms the event and the cited report’s identity. A television appearance has limited value as evidence of a formal appointment.

rows.source: Periods for notice and appeal in the 2025 disciplinary rules
rows.usage: Paraphrase of original passage. CMR-58, PDF p. 15, paragraph immediately before Figure 3 and note 58. The report gives separate 30-day periods for notice of the decision and appeal.
rows.finding: The report cites a translation of the 2018 trial text at the figure. The 2025 announcement confirms revised rules were issued, but does not state the clock or the notice exceptions. The operative 2025 articles are needed for both deadlines. Source recheck. Articles 132 and 173 in the recovered 2025 text separately support the two reported periods. The announcement clock runs from the decision, while the appeal clock runs from announcement. Article 132 also gives exceptions to the standard manner of announcement.

rows.source: Effectiveness of the 2018 trial disciplinary rules
rows.usage: Paraphrase of original passage. CMR-58, PDF p. 15, paragraph after Figure 3. The report identifies trial disciplinary regulations that took effect in 2018.
rows.finding: The defense ministry’s 2018 promulgation identifies the revised discipline text as a trial regulation and specifies May 1, 2018 as the effective date. This was the prior instrument referred to in the passage.

rows.source: Discipline commission among the bodies in the CMC’s 2016 restructuring
rows.usage: Paraphrase of original passage. CMR-58, PDF p. 4, institutional reorganization discussion, note 5. The report describes elevation of the discipline function into the reorganized CMC structure.
rows.finding: The defense ministry’s contemporary briefing identifies the discipline inspection commission in the new central organization. That supports the formal reorganization. The resulting pattern of actual reporting is a separate institutional claim.
evidence: Defense ministry restructuring briefing, Xinhua archive

rows.source: Source edition for the reported range of disciplinary sanctions
rows.usage: Paraphrase of original passage. CMR-58, PDF p. 17, statement of potential sanctions, note 66. The report lists warnings, demerits, demotions and dismissal among possible outcomes.
rows.finding: The cited translation is dated 2023 and therefore predates the April 2025 rules discussed earlier. The public 2018 trial text can establish the earlier sanction categories. A pinpoint to the applicable 2025 categories and decision authorities is needed for a current claim. Source recheck. Articles 90–92 provide distinct sanction lists by personnel category. The English summary should distinguish warnings, demerits and changes to grade or rank from removal or expulsion. Use the applicable 2025 list and its personnel category for the current edition. The 2023 translation cannot establish the revised classification.

paper_memo.memo_title: One-Page Analytical Memo — CMR-58: Tightening the Institutional Cage: The PLA Navy's Discipline Inspection Commission (Eric Hundman & Connor Akiyama, Sept 28, 2026)

sections.heading: 1. Strategic Context & Core Thesis
sections.body: Published on September 28, 2026 as China Maritime Report No. 58 by Dr. Eric Hundman (Director of Research at BluePath Labs) and Connor Akiyama (Civilian Analyst at the U.S. Department of the Navy), this 20-page monograph is the chronological capstone of the dashboard. Hundman and Akiyama provide the first dedicated open-source institutional study of the PLA Navy Headquarters Discipline Inspection Commission (PLAN DIC / 海军纪律检查委员会) and its subordinate fleet/base DICs. They argue that since the 2016 PLA reforms—which detached the CMC DIC from the dissolved General Political Department and elevated its secretary (Gen. Zhang Shengmin) onto the CMC as a direct reporting channel to Xi Jinping—the PLAN DIC has expanded its remit from hunting high-level corrupt 'tigers' to 'tightening the institutional cage' (扎紧制度笼子) around grassroots sailors across political loyalty, training effort, financial/welfare rules, and NCO selection. Yet this pervasive surveillance faces persistent case-processing backlogs, provokes passive resistance among units, and recently saw two career legal/disciplinary professionals (Liu Xunyan and Cheng Dongfang) replaced at the top by a Rocket Force political officer (VADM Chen Hongke), signaling that Xi Jinping prioritizes personal political loyalty ('redness') over technocratic investigative pedigree.

sections.heading: 2. Section-by-Section Analytical Breakdown
sections.body:
• Sections 1 & 2 (CMC DIC Centralization, PLAN DIC vs. PLAC Division of Labor & Six Disciplinary Priorities, pp. 1-6): Traces the PLA DIC system from 1981 to the 2016 'above-the-neck' reforms. Clarifies a key institutional boundary at PLAN Headquarters: security/counterintelligence, military procuratorates, and military courts belong to the PLAN Politics and Legal Affairs Commission (PLAC, typically chaired by the first-ranked PLAN Deputy Political Commissar), whereas the PLAN DIC (typically chaired by the second-ranked PLAN Deputy Political Commissar, who concurrently serves as Supervisory Committee Secretary) enforces Party discipline, combats the 'Four Malpractices' (四风: formalism, bureaucratism, hedonism, extravagance), and transfers bribery/embezzlement cases exceeding the **30,000 RMB (~$4,100 USD) redline** to the military judiciary. Citing a Southern Theater Command Navy DIC special inspection notice (dated Sept 2023 in Note 19, though misdated '2020' in the text), the authors detail six active priorities: (1) political discipline and policy implementation; (2) inspection organization and lack of interest in training; (3) the Four Malpractices (public funds, gifts, lavish weddings/funerals); (4) infringing on sailors' rights, bribes for home leave, drunk driving, and online gambling; (5) excessive housing/vehicle perks; and (6) general work-style rectification, enforced at the unit level via the 'First Form' (第一种形态) and appointed **'grassroots atmosphere supervisors' (基层风气监督员)**.

• Section 3 (Internal Structure & the Seven PLAN DIC Secretaries Since 2012, pp. 6-11): Identifies three confirmed sub-units of the PLAN Headquarters DIC—the **Inspection and Supervision Bureau (纪检监察局)**, the **Case Handling and Support/Security Office (办案保障室)**, and the **Case Hearing Department (案件审理处)**, plus the 2011 Cadre Training Base—and notes that 11 members were elected to the PLAN DIC at the 12th PLAN Party Congress (May 2017) and 10 members at the 13th Congress (June 2022). Traces the seven PLAN DIC Secretaries since 2012: Cen Xu, Wang Sentai, Wang Dengping, Chen Xuebin, **VADM Liu Xunyan** (2017-2024/2025, a former PLAAF/GPD Security Dept and CMC PLAC deputy secretary who was the first career disciplinary investigator in the post), **VADM Cheng Dongfang** (former PLA Military Court President and CMC PLAC Deputy Secretary, who went missing in early 2025), and **VADM Chen Hongke** (a career PLA Rocket Force political officer and former PC of Rocket Force Engineering University, serving as of early 2026).

• Sections 4 & 5 (The 2025 PLA Discipline Regulations Flowchart, Case Backlogs, Personnel Vetting & Passive Resistance, pp. 12-18): Maps the statutory investigation process under the **Discipline Regulations of the PLA (2025)** (effective April 2025, Fig. 3): **45 days** for the DIC to verify facts and the Party Committee to decide on punishment, **30 days** to announce the decision, and **30 days** for appeal (with expanded wartime summary powers for lower-grade and temporary units). In practice, however, a Sept 2022 *People's Navy* report on a **'100-day zero-clear campaign' (百日清零会战)** shows cases routinely exceeded 45 days. Beyond investigations, the PLAN DIC supervises annual Senior NCO selection boards, implements the CMC **'Indicator System' (指标体系)** grading party committees into four tiers (*excellent, good, average, ineffective*), and produces propaganda films. While PLAN DIC Bureau Director Wu Wei boasted in 2022 that 'We have tightened the institutional cage, leaving no windows or back doors,' the authors document resulting **passive resistance**—citing a 2024 *PLA Daily* admission of 'lukewarm approaches to rectification, characterized by superficial efforts and delays' and an April 2024 *People's Navy* report on a frigate detachment transferring 2 insufficiently dedicated cadres and 9 rule-violating cadres.

sections.heading: 3. Key Doctrinal Concepts, Terminology & Quantitative Claims
sections.body:
• Core Disciplinary Formulations: 'Tightening the institutional cage' (扎紧制度笼子); 'The Four Malpractices / Four Winds' (四风: formalism, bureaucratism, hedonism, extravagance); 'The First Form' (第一种形态) & 'Grassroots atmosphere supervisors' (基层风气监督员); '100-day zero-clear campaign' (百日清零会战); and the CMC Party Committee 'Indicator System' (指标体系).
• Key Statutory & Quantitative Benchmarks: 30,000 RMB (~$4,100 USD) judicial transfer redline; 11 elected PLAN DIC members (2017) & 10 elected members (2022); 7 PLAN DIC Secretaries since 2012; 2025 PLA Discipline Regulations timelines = 45 days to decide + 30 days to announce + 30 days to appeal; Northern Theater Navy DIC online training = >200 DIC cadres + 800 key personnel.

sections.heading: 4. Audit Assessment & Analytical Significance
sections.body:
Of the 4 reference rows in CMR-58, 3 are rated ok and 1 is rated fix ([CMR58-R02]): our cross-check between the main text, the footnotes, and CMR-57 caught three chronological errors where the main text misstates the year of the source cited in its own footnote—misdating the **September 26, 2023** Southern Theater Navy DIC inspection (Note 19) to **'2020'** on p. 5; misdating a **March 2021** report on the CMC 'First Form' notice (Note 21) to **'the beginning of 2024'** on p. 6; and misdating the **2019** warning film *The Disaster of Greed* (Note 74) to **'2021'** on p. 16. We also logged minor slips in Figure 3 on p. 13 ('punihsment', 'deicison', 'exceedes', and Note 58 citing the 2018 Trial Regulations URL) and Note 15 ('13 July 2019' for 13 Jan 2019). Analytically, CMR-58 completes the Party-military governance triad with CMR-56 and CMR-57, showing how the CCP polices the PLAN from top flag officers down to frigate detachments.

**Footnote rows**: all 83 footnotes were extracted and consolidated into 75 source rows in the Reference Audit Matrix (CMR58-N001 to CMR58-N083). Repeat citations of the same source within this paper, including Ibid. and short-form notes, share one row, which lists each note's passage and result. Footnote-level result: 83 notes: 6 (7%) are confirmed, 1 of them against a retrieved source and 5 after an outside web search (4 of the latter with a slip or an unchecked detail noted); 2 are flagged for reader check; 77 (93%) are not confirmed. Of the 77 notes not confirmed, 52 are Chinese-language sources that have not been searched in Chinese (a search in Chinese could settle some of them); 1 was judged not web-checkable (1 note that is a fragment or run-on text attached to a Chinese-language source); 24 were searched on the web without finding corroboration. A source row is `ok` only when every note in it is confirmed, and `fix` when a note is confirmed wrong; the paper's 75 source rows are 5 `ok`, 0 `fix` and 70 `unk`. Notes flagged for reader check, for example (the outside search found something a reader should look at; none is a finding that the author is wrong): `CMR58-N019`: The sentence says a 2020 special inspection by the Southern Theater Command Navy DIC set out six priorities; the cited page (Tencent News, 26 September 2023) describes a 2023 inspection around the Mid-Autumn Festival and National Day with six focus areas of a similar kind; `CMR58-N058`: The figure caption refers to the 2025 Discipline Regulations, but the note as it appears in the dataset cites China Law Translate's translation of the 2018 regulations. 4 notes carry a reader note on how the note is displayed or cited.
